events.title: Daniel and His Friends Taken to Babylon
events.description: King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon besieges Jerusalem and takes King Jehoiakim captive. Among those taken are Daniel and his three friends Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, who are given the Babylonian names Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. They are chosen for training at the king's court but refuse to eat the king's food and wine. After a ten-day test, they appear healthier than the others, and God gives them knowledge and wisdom.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Statue
events.description: Nebuchadnezzar has a troubling dream and demands that the wise men not only interpret the dream but also tell him what he dreamed. No one can do this, so the king orders all the wise men to be executed. Daniel prays to God and receives the dream revealed in a night vision. The dream concerns a great statue with a head of gold, chest of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, and feet of iron mixed with clay, which is crushed by a stone. Daniel explains that the statue represents four world empires, all of which will perish, but God's kingdom will endure forever.

events.title: The Fiery Furnace – Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego
events.description: Nebuchadnezzar erects a massive golden statue on the plain of Dura and commands that all must worship it when music plays. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse to bow before the idol. The king becomes furious and orders the furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. The three men are thrown into the blazing furnace, but to the king's astonishment, he sees four men walking freely among the flames—the fourth looks like a son of the gods. The three are brought out unharmed from the furnace without even smelling of smoke, and the king praises their God.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar's Madness
events.description: Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a mighty tree reaching up to heaven and giving shelter to all living creatures, but a watcher commands that the tree be cut down. Daniel interprets the dream with sorrow: the tree is the king himself, and he will be driven away from people and live among animals for seven times until he acknowledges that the Most High rules over human kingdoms. Twelve months later the king boasts of his greatness, and judgment falls immediately. After seven times Nebuchadnezzar's reason returns, and he praises and honors the God of heaven.

events.title: The Writing on the Wall – Belshazzar's Feast
events.description: King Belshazzar holds a grand feast for a thousand of his nobles and drinks wine from the holy vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem. Suddenly, a hand appears and writes on the wall. The king is terrified and calls for the wise men, but none can interpret the writing. The queen mother suggests Daniel. He reads the words MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UFARSIN and interprets them: God has numbered Belshazzar's kingdom and brought it to an end; the king has been weighed and found wanting; and his kingdom will be divided between the Medes and Persians. That same night Belshazzar is killed, and Darius the Mede takes over the kingdom.

events.title: Daniel in the Lions' Den
events.description: Darius sets Daniel as one of three royal advisors over the entire kingdom. The other officials become jealous and find no fault in Daniel, so they persuade the king to issue a decree forbidding prayer to anyone except the king for thirty days. Daniel continues to pray to his God three times daily with windows open toward Jerusalem. He is accused and thrown into the lions' den. The king spends a sleepless night, and at dawn he finds Daniel unharmed – God had sent his angel to shut the lions' mouths. Daniel's accusers are cast into the den and torn apart.

events.title: The Vision of the Four Beasts
events.description: In the first year of Belshazzar's reign, Daniel sees a vision of four great beasts rising from the sea: a lion with eagle wings, a bear, a leopard with four wings and four heads, and a fourth terrifying beast with iron teeth and ten horns. A little horn grows up and speaks proud words. Daniel sees the Ancient of Days take his seat on the throne, and one like a son of man is brought before him and given eternal dominion over all peoples and nations. An angel explains that the beasts represent four kingdoms, but the holy ones of the Most High will receive the kingdom forever.

events.title: The Vision of the Ram and the Goat
events.description: In the third year of King Belshazzar's reign, Daniel sees a vision by the Ulai River in Susa. He sees a ram with two horns pushing westward, northward, and southward—no one can stand against it. Then a male goat comes from the west with a large horn between its eyes, which shatters the ram. But when the goat is at its strongest, the large horn breaks off and is replaced by four horns. From one of them grows a small horn that turns toward the Beautiful Land and exalts itself against the host of heaven. The angel Gabriel explains that the ram represents the kings of Media and Persia, the goat represents the king of Greece, and the small horn represents a coming tyrannical king.

events.title: Daniel's Prayer and the Seventy Weeks
events.description: In the first year of Darius's reign, Daniel understands from Jeremiah's prophecy that Jerusalem's desolation will last seventy years. He turns to God in prayer and fasting, confesses the people's sins, and asks for mercy over Jerusalem and the temple. While he is still praying, the angel Gabriel flies to him at the time of the evening sacrifice. Gabriel reveals the prophecy of the seventy weeks – 490 years – which are decreed for Daniel's people and the holy city: to put an end to transgression, to make atonement for sin, to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to anoint the most holy place.

events.title: The Great Vision
events.description: In the third year of Cyrus's reign, Daniel receives a comprehensive vision after three weeks of mourning and fasting by the Tigris River. A figure clothed in linen, with a face like lightning and eyes like flaming torches, appears to him. Daniel falls to the ground, but the figure strengthens him and reveals what will happen to his people in the last days. The vision describes in detail coming conflicts between kings of the north and south, the abominable desolation, and a time of distress unlike any before. Finally, it is promised that those written in the book will be saved, the dead will rise, and the wise will shine like the firmament.
